content: The administration of booster doses is recommended to include combination vaccines containing tetanus toxoid (TT) and diphtheria toxoid, as opposed to single-antigen vaccines, whenever feasible. The effectiveness of at least two properly timed doses of TT administered to pregnant women or women of reproductive age in preventing neonatal tetanus (NT) mortality is estimated at 94% (95% CI: 80–98%). Despite the availability of highly effective TT-containing vaccines, tetanus continues to pose a significant global health burden. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), in 2018, approximately 25,000 newborns died from neonatal tetanus. While this represents an 88% reduction from the estimated 200,000 deaths in the year 2000, the Maternal and Neonatal Tetanus Elimination (MNTE) initiative still faces numerous challenges. Approximately 47 million women and their infants remain unprotected against tetanus. Timeliness of case investigation is critical, with a target of investigating at least 80% of suspected cases within seven days of notification. Adequacy of investigation is defined as the percentage of cases investigated with complete information on all 12 core variables, also with a target of ≥80%. These core variables include case identification, date of birth, sex, place of residence, date of illness onset, date of notification, date of investigation, symptoms meeting the case definition, outcome, maternal vaccination history, place/type of delivery, tool used for cutting the umbilical cord, and materials applied to the cord. If any of these variables are missing, the investigation is considered inadequate. To maintain MNTE, the target is for 100% of districts to report fewer than one NT case per 1,000 live births. Ideally, this indicator should be calculated using confirmed cases. Additionally, an adequate case response involves ensuring that 100% of mothers of confirmed NT cases receive a TT-containing vaccine (TTCV) dose during case detection or investigation. The document was developed under the strategic guidance of Dr. Poonam Khetrapal Singh, Regional Director of WHO South-East Asia, and other senior WHO officials, including Dr. Pem Namgyal and Dr. Suman Rijal. The process was overseen by Dr. Sunil Bahl, Coordinator of COVAX, Immunization, and Vaccines Development, with technical coordination led by Dr. Sudhir Khanal and Dr. Sudhir Joshi. WHO consultant Dr. Lalit Kant played a key role in updating the technical content. The document also benefited from expert input from participants of the Regional Workshop on Measles-Rubella and Vaccine-Preventable Disease (VPD) Surveillance, held in Dhaka in June 2022. This included contributions from National EPI Program Managers, VPD Surveillance Officers, WHO country office staff, UNICEF representatives, and other external collaborators. WHO headquarters staff, including Dr. Anindya Bose and Dr. Heidi Soeters, reviewed the draft and provided technical inputs. Additional contributions were made by WHO South-East Asia Regional Office staff, UNICEF representatives (led by Christopher Gregory), and US CDC experts, including Dr. Ahmed Kassem and Dr. Michelle Morales, who coordinated inputs from various teams.
